text: If it feels comfortable, let your breathing slow naturally. You might make the out-breath a little longer than the in-breath, without forcing it.
Try noticing one breath at a time. If focusing on breath feels uncomfortable, stop and orient to something you can see instead.
Look around and name five things you see, four things you feel, and three things you hear. Take your time; this is an optional attention exercise.
Press your feet gently into the floor and notice where your body is supported. You can stop if this does not feel helpful.
Choose an object nearby and describe its color, shape, texture, and weight to yourself, bringing attention back to the present surroundings.
Name the day, where you are, and one small thing you plan to do next. Simple orientation can help anchor attention.
Hold a cool or textured object and describe the sensation. Keep the exercise gentle and skip it if it increases discomfort.
A small, flexible daily rhythm can make the day feel more manageable. Consider choosing one regular time for a meal, rest, or a short walk.
Break a demanding task into one very small next step. It is okay to pause and revise the plan.
Choose one realistic task for today and one thing you can postpone. A shorter list can reduce pressure.
A consistent sleep and wake schedule may support a steadier routine. Aim for a routine that is realistic for your circumstances.
If possible, make the sleeping space quiet, dim, and comfortable. Small changes are optional; do what is practical for you.
Consider a gentle wind-down activity before bed, such as quiet music or reading, and reduce bright screens if that suits you.
If sleep remains difficult or affects daily life, consider discussing it with a qualified health professional.
You could send a brief message to someone you trust, such as, “I have had a hard day. Could we talk for a few minutes?”
If talking feels difficult, spending quiet time near a trusted person can still be a form of connection.
Consider identifying one person, community group, or professional service you could contact if you need support.
If it is safe and accessible, a few minutes of gentle movement or walking may be a useful change of pace. Rest is also okay.
Try stretching only within a comfortable range. Do not push through pain, and choose another activity if movement is not suitable.
Notice one activity you are doing right now, and gently bring attention back when your mind wanders. There is no need to do it perfectly.
Pause and notice one sound, one color, and one physical sensation. This is a brief attention practice, not a way to solve every problem.
Try speaking to yourself as you might speak to a friend who is having a difficult day: with patience rather than blame.
A difficult feeling does not mean you have failed. You can acknowledge it and choose one manageable next step.
Write down what is on your mind, then mark one item that can wait. You do not need to solve everything at once.
For a stressful task, consider what is in your control today and what is not. Focus on one controllable action if that feels useful.
If news or social media leaves you feeling more tense, consider taking a short break or choosing a limited time to check updates.
If you can, consider having some water and a regular meal. Everyday needs can be harder to notice when you feel overwhelmed.
A short pause can be useful. Choose a comfortable place, let your shoulders rest, and decide later what you want to do next.
Think of one small action that reflects something important to you, such as kindness, learning, or connection. Keep it achievable.
Describe the problem in one sentence, list a few possible next steps, and choose the smallest safe step. You can ask someone you trust to help.
If distress is persistent, worsening, or interfering with daily life, a qualified mental-health professional can help assess what support may fit.
You do not need to wait until things feel unbearable to ask for help. Consider contacting a clinician or trusted support person.
If you may be in immediate danger, contact your local emergency service now and reach out to a trusted person who can stay with you.
If you are in India and need urgent mental-health support, Tele-MANAS can be reached at 14416. If danger is immediate, use local emergency services.
You can skip any exercise that does not suit you. Choose what feels manageable, or simply tell someone you trust what is happening.
